<p class="proj-lead">
How much does the murder rate of a US state move with its robbery rate? The answer depends on how much shape you let the data have. I fitted a straight line, a kernel smoother and local polynomials to the state averages of the Stock and Watson `Guns` panel, chose the smoothing by cross-validation, and compared them on data left out.
</p>

<div class="proj-stats">
  <div class="proj-stat"><b>1,173</b><span>state-years, 51 states from 1977 to 1999, averaged by state</span></div>
  <div class="proj-stat"><b>50</b><span>states in the fit, after removing the District of Columbia</span></div>
  <div class="proj-stat"><b>12.7</b><span>bandwidth of the kernel smoother, chosen by cross-validation</span></div>
  <div class="proj-stat"><b>7.0 vs 7.7</b><span>average test error of the local linear fit against the straight line</span></div>
</div>

<p class="proj-meta">Course project, Advanced Statistics for Finance, Sapienza University of Rome, July 2025. R, estimatr, np, glmnet, leaps.</p>

## The data and the line

Averaging each state over the 23 years gives one point per state. The District of Columbia sits far from the rest, at a murder rate of 49.3 per 100,000, and has a large influence on every fit, so I removed it. On the remaining 50 states the straight line has a slope of 0.0219 murders per 100,000 for each additional robbery per 100,000 and explains 42% of the variance. Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (HC2) put the slope's standard error at 0.0040 against 0.0037 for the classical one: the conclusion does not change, the interval is a little wider.

## Letting the data choose the shape

The Nadaraya–Watson estimator is a local weighted average of the murder rates, with weights that depend on how close each state's robbery rate is to the point being estimated. How close is "close" is the bandwidth $$h$$: small values chase individual states, large ones flatten towards the global mean. Minimising the in-sample error cannot choose it, because the error is smallest when $$h$$ goes to zero and the curve passes through every point; so $$h$$ is chosen by leave-one-out cross-validation, with a shortcut that avoids refitting the model 50 times.

```r
nw <- function(x, X, Y, h, K = dnorm) {
  Kx <- rbind(sapply(X, function(Xi) K((x - Xi) / h) / h))   # kernel weight of every point, for every x
  W  <- Kx / rowSums(Kx)                                     # weights that sum to one
  drop(W %*% Y)                                              # a local weighted average of Y
}

# leave-one-out error without refitting n times: divide each residual by (1 - its own weight)
cv_nw <- function(X, Y, h, K = dnorm) {
  Kh     <- outer(X, X, function(xi, xj) K((xi - xj) / h))
  fhat   <- Kh %*% Y / rowSums(Kh)
  W_diag <- K(0) / rowSums(Kh)
  mean(((Y - fhat) / (1 - W_diag))^2)
}
```

<div class="caption">Murder against robbery rate for 50 states. Move the slider to change the bandwidth of the kernel fit; the dashed line is the bandwidth chosen by cross-validation, the dotted line the straight line.</div>

I chose the bandwidth in two ways: a grid search over my own implementation of the leave-one-out error, and the cross-validation routine of the `np` package. On the 50 states they give 17.8 and 12.7. The grid search's minimum is the smallest bandwidth at which the shortcut can be computed: below about 17.8 the state with the highest robbery rate has no neighbour within reach, its weight on itself is 1, and its leave-one-out error is 0/0. The `np` routine copes with that and puts the minimum at 12.7. With the District of Columbia left in, my grid search went to 68.2 against 15.2 for `np`: isolated points move the hand-made criterion much more than the package's, which is why I adopted the package's choice after removing it.

<div class="caption">Leave-one-out error of the kernel fit as a function of the bandwidth. The shortcut is not defined in the grey region; the dashed line is the bandwidth chosen by the np package.</div>

## Which fit predicts best?

To compare the methods fairly I split the 50 states 100 times at random, 80% for fitting and 20% for testing, and averaged the squared prediction error of each method over the splits: a straight line, the kernel fit with its own cross-validated bandwidth, and loess with local linear and local quadratic fits.

| method                   | average test MSE |
| :----------------------- | ---------------: |
| straight line            |             7.66 |
| kernel (Nadaraya–Watson) |             7.09 |
| loess, local linear      |             6.98 |
| loess, local quadratic   |             7.45 |

The four are close, with the local linear fit lowest and the kernel estimator next, and the errors of the mean over the 100 splits are about 0.3 each: the data ask for a little flexibility more than a straight line, not much.

## A second question: what predicts incarceration?

The same state averages can be asked a different question: which variables predict the incarceration rate? A robust linear model on all the other variables finds `murder` the only one that is statistically significant. Forward selection with BIC keeps one variable, `murder`; the lasso, with the penalty chosen by 10-fold cross-validation, keeps three: `murder`, `violent` and `afam`. Refitting a linear model on those three, `murder` is still the only significant one. Both methods agree on the variable that matters, and differ on how much else to include.
